title: The History of Deep Dish Pizza — The "Pizza" Real Italians Refuse to Call Pizza
fullText: In 1884, chalera tore through the port city of Naples, Italy, killing over 7,000 people in a matter of months, according to official cemetery records that historians now believe underounted the true toll by a wide margin. The disease moved through the city's poorest quarters first, through the cramped, sunless alleys known as the basi, where entire families lived, cooked, and slept in a single windowless room. City officials panicked. Thousands fled. King Ombberto I eventually toured the infected districts in a show of royal concern. Though he was careful, according to contemporary accounts, to keep his visit brief and his distance wide. The slums he walked through were some of the most crowded, most desperate streets in all of Europe. And yet, in those same streets, something else was happening. Street vendors were selling a cheap, fast, filling flatbread for pennies a piece. A food so associated with poverty that wealthy Neapolitans considered it beneath them and so ordinary that nobody thought to write its history down. That food was pizza. Today, a single Chicago style deep dish pizza can cost over $35, takes nearly an hour to bake, arrives with a knife and fork, and is, according to a great many actual Neapolitans, not really pizza at all. So, how did a peasant food born in the slums of a chalera stricken city become on one side of the Atlantic a UNESCO protected cultural treasure defended by law and on the other side a deep pan cheese buried casserole invented in 1943 by a liquor salesman from Texas who was originally trying to open a Mexican restaurant. That was 1884. But the story of pizza does not begin with kalera or with kings or even with Italy as a unified country because in the century before that epidemic Naples was not yet part of Italy at all. It was the capital of its own kingdom and it was already quietly becoming the birthplace of the most eaten food on earth. Pizza's ancestors go back much further than Naples. Of course, flatbreads cooked on hot stones existed across the ancient Mediterranean. In Egypt, in Greece in Rome, wherever people had grain, water, and fire, ancient Greeks ate a flatbread called pluse, topped with oil, herbs, and cheese. The Romans had something similar. None of this was pizza in any meaningful sense. Though food writers love to draw the line anyway, because a flat piece of bread with something on top is honestly one of the most obvious inventions in human history. It required no genius, no epiphany, just people with wheat [music] and no easy way to bake a loaf. What actually turned this ordinary flatbread into pizza did not happen in a palace or a monastery. It happened among the poorest residents of one specific city, and it took roughly two centuries to unfold. Naples had a few advantages that most of the rest of Europe simply did not. It sat on the Bay of Naples, one of the most fertile stretches of coastline on the Italian peninsula with volcanic soil from Mount Vuvius, producing wheat, olive oil, and eventually tomatoes in far greater abundance than most inland cities could manage. It was also by the 17th and 18th centuries, one of the most densely populated cities in all of Europe, packed well beyond its infrastructure, which meant an enormous permanent population of laborers who needed to eat constantly, cheaply, and without ceremony. Bakers in Naples did not know the word marketing, and they certainly did not think of themselves as building a global cuisine. They were solving a much smaller, much more immediate problem. How to keep an entire underclass fed on almost no money using an oven, some flour, and whatever cheap toppings happened to be available that week. Some vendors used lard and cheese. Some used tiny fish called chachchingelli. Some, particularly during Lent, made a version with nothing but garlic, oil, and oregano, a stripped down style that still exists today under the name pizza marinara, named not for seafood, but for the fisherman's wives. the Marinari, who traditionally made it for their husbands, returning hungry from weeks at sea. None of these early pizzas were designed to impress anyone. They were designed to be eaten in under 2 minutes by someone who needed to get back to work. By the 1500s, round flatbreads called pizza were already a fixture of Neapolitan street life, sold hot, folded, and cheap to a population that needed food it could eat while standing, working, or walking. Naples at the time was one of the largest cities in Europe and also one of the poorest packed with a permanent underclass known as the Lzeroni, day laborers, dock workers, and street peddlers who lived hand-to-mouth in the literal sense. These were people without kitchens, in many cases without regular income, who needed calories that were fast, filling, and did not require a table. Pizza met every one of those requirements. It cost almost nothing. It needed no plate, and a communal wood-fired oven could turn out enough of it to feed an entire neighborhood in an afternoon. This was not a delicacy. This was survival food, and the people eating it were judged for it. Educated Italian writers of the period described the eating habits of the Naples poor as disgusting, according to food historians who have studied the era's writing. And travelers who wandered into the slums to gawk at the strange, quick eating habits of the Lzeroni treated pizza the way a modern tourist might treat an unfamiliar street snack in a country they consider beneath them. Nobody involved in cooking or eating this food had any idea that within 200 years it would be the single most recognized meal on the planet. Here is the detail that changes everything about this story. Though for most of pizza's early life, it did not have tomatoes on it at all. Because Europe did not have tomatoes. Tomatoes are native to the Americas. And when Spanish explorers brought them back across the Atlantic in the 1500s, most of Europe looked at this strange red fruit and assumed it was poisonous. Wealthy households grew tomatoes as an ornamental curiosity, not as food. It was the poor of Naples, again, who broke the taboo because they had less to lose and less patience for aristocratic squeamishness about a plant that was, it turned out, perfectly edible and delicious on bread. By the late 1700s, Neapolitan street vendors were topping their flatbreads with tomatoes and pizza, as the world would eventually recognize it, had arrived. Not because a chef designed it, not because a monarch ordered it, because hungry people needed a quick meal and decided the fruit everyone else was afraid of tasted fine. By 1807, there were already 54 registered pizzeras operating in Naples, and that number roughly doubled within a few decades. One of them, a spot called Port Alba, had started as a street stall back in 1738, cooking flatbreads in ovens lined with volcanic stone. And by 1830, it had become a full sit-down restaurant. It is still open today, and it is widely considered the oldest pizzeria in the world. Think about that for a second. A food that started as an embarrassment, something the upper classes would not be caught eating, had built an entire commercial industry around itself in one city decades before pizza existed anywhere else on the planet. This is where the most famous pizza origin story comes in. The one printed on menus and repeated in a thousand travel articles, and it deserves to be told honestly, myth label and all. The most popular version goes like this. In 1889, 5 years after that chalera epidemic swept through the city, King Ombberto I and his wife, Queen Margarita of Seavoi made another visit to Naples. According to the legend, the queen had grown tired of the rich French-style cuisine that dominated European royal dining at the time, and she asked to try the local food the ordinary people of Naples actually ate. A pizzolo named Raphael Esposito working at a restaurant that would later be renamed Pizzeria Brandy supposedly created a pizza specifically for her. Topped with red tomatoes, white mozzarella, and green basil. The three colors of the newly unified Italian flag. The queen loved it, the story goes, and Esposito named it in her honor, Pizza Margarita. Now, historians who have dug into the archives have found real problems with this tidy narrative. A text from 1849, a full 40 years before the supposed royal visit, already describes a pizza topped with basil, tomato, and mozzarella arranged in the shape of a flower. Some food historians argue this exact tomato, cheese, and basil combination existed in Naples as early as the late 1700s, decades before any queen tasted it. So, the truth is almost certainly that Esposito did not invent the margarita. He may have simply served an already existing style of pizza to a member of the royal family who happened to enjoy it, and a very good marketing story did the rest. Whether every detail of the queen's visit is historically accurate remains genuinely debated among food historians, but the result is beyond dispute. The connection to Italian royalty gave a poor person's street food the one thing it had never had before, respectability. And it took a queen's name being attached to a peasant dish for the wealthy of Naples to stop looking down on it. give you half that woman. Pay attention to this next detail because it explains almost everything that happens later in this story. Pizza's entire identity from the very beginning was built on being cheap, fast, and unpretentious. A thin, blistered crust that could be cooked in 90 seconds in an oven blasting past 800° F. A handful of toppings, nothing piled on, nothing hidden. This was not a dish designed to be filling in the American sense. It was designed to be eaten quickly, standing up by people with almost no money and almost no time. That specific identity, thin, fast, minimal, would later collide head-on with an entirely different idea of what pizza was supposed to be 4,000 m away and about 200 years later. This decision, this original recipe for what pizza fundamentally was seemed permanent at the time. It was not. Pizza did not stay in Naples forever, obviously, and its journey out of Italy tells you almost as much about immigration and prejudice in America as it does about food. Beginning in the late 1800s, waves of Italian immigrants, many of them from the exact same poor communities in and around Naples that had invented pizza in the first place, began arriving in the United States by the millions, fleeing overcrowding, poverty, and a fractured Italian economy that had not caught up with the rest of unifying Italy. They brought their food with them because that is what immigrants do. They carry the one thing nobody can take away. In New York City's Little Italy, peddlers began selling pizza on the street for two cents a slice, exactly the way it had been sold back home. A cheap, fast meal for a population of laborers with very little money and very long work days. In 1905, a baker named Jaro Lombardi opened what is generally credited as the first licensed pizzeria in the United States on Spring Street in Manhattan. For decades after that, pizza remained almost entirely confined to Italian immigrant neighborhoods. It was not American food. It was ethnic food eaten by and largely for one specific community. And most of the country had never tasted it and had no particular interest in trying. Picture what that actually looked like on the street. Coal fired ovens built into tenement basement. The smell of scorched flour and simmering tomato drifting up through the sidewalk grates of Malberry Street and Spring Street. Vendors wrapping hot slices in brown paper for laborers who ate standing on the corner because they had nowhere else to eat and no time to sit down even if they did. This was immigrant food in the truest sense. Cooked by people who had nothing. Sold to people who had almost nothing. entirely invisible to the wealthier, largely Protestant America that dominated the country's cultural conversation at the time. Millions of Italians made this same journey between 1880 and the early 1900s part of one of the largest waves of immigration in American history. And they did not arrive to gratitude for the food, the language, or the culture they brought with them. They arrived to suspicion. Here is the uncomfortable reality that gets left out of most pizza histories, and it deserves to be said with the seriousness it warrants. The Italian immigrants who brought pizza to America did not arrive to open arms. They arrived into a country in the grip of serious, often violent anti-Italian prejudice. On March the 14th, 1891, a mob of thousands stormed the parish prison in New Orleans and murdered 11 Italian immigrants who had been accused without real evidence of killing the city's police chief. Several of the men had already been acquitted by a jury. It did not matter. The mob dragged them out, shot them, and hung two of the bodies from a lamp post and a tree while a crowd of thousands watched. It remains to this day the largest single mass lynching in American history and its victims were Italian. Between 1880 and 1921, historians have documented at least 50 separate cases of Italians being lynched across nine different American states. Italian immigrants during this period were frequently described in American newspapers using the same dehumanizing racial language used against black Americans and they were widely regarded as racially suspect, criminally inclined and unfit for full citizenship. This was not fringe sentiment. It ran through respectable society, through newspapers, through elected officials. This was the environment pizza grew up in on American soil. Not a warm welcome, but decades of suspicion and violence directed at the very people who cooked it. Pizza did not conquer America because America was eager for it. It survived in the margins in immigrant kitchens for nearly half a century, while the country that would eventually fall in love with it treated the people who made it as barely tolerated outsiders. That suspicion did not end with the 1800s either. And this next detail tends to surprise people because it happened well within living memory of the deep dish story that follows. When the United States entered World War II against Italy, Germany, and Japan in December of 1941, the federal government classified more than 600,000 Italian-born residents of the United States, most of them longtime immigrants who had simply never gotten around to filing citizenship paperwork, as enemy aliens. They were required to carry government identification cards at all times. Forbidden from owning radios, cameras, or flashlights, and along the West Coast, placed under a strict curfew that confined them to their homes between 8:00 in the evening and 6:00 in the morning and barred them from traveling more than 5 miles without written permission. Joe Deaggio's own father, a fisherman in San Francisco, was barred from the waterfront where he had worked for decades and had his boat confiscated. one small telling detail among hundreds of thousands of similar stories. More than 10,000 Italian-Ameans were forced from their homes entirely and several hundred were sent to internment camps in states like Montana, Texas, and Tennessee. This happened at the exact same moment American soldiers, the sons and neighbors of these same targeted communities, were fighting their way up the Italian peninsula and discovering pizza for the first time in the towns their own government was treating their relatives as suspects for coming from. It is a strange, almost cruel irony sitting right at the center of this story. The dish that would go on to conquer American appetites was falling in love with the country at the exact moment that country was locking up the people who had given it that dish in the first place. This is where the story takes a turn nobody expected and it involves a war. World War II sent hundreds of thousands of American soldiers to fight their way up the Italian peninsula between 1943 and 1945 through Sicily, through Naples, through Rome. For many of these young men, most of whom had never left the United States before, this was their first encounter with pizza, eaten hot from wood-fired ovens in the same city where the dish had been invented roughly a century and a half earlier. They came home changed, and one of the things that changed was their appetite. Returning veterans who had eaten pizza in Italy started asking for it in the United States. And suddenly a food that had been confined to Italian immigrant enclaves for 40 years had a much wider, much hungrier American audience. This is the exact moment this precise gap between wartime exposure and a country suddenly primed for something new that a Texan liquor salesman with no restaurant experience decided to open a pizzeria in Chicago. And this next part is where the surprising twist in this whole story actually lives. If you are finding this interesting, hit subscribe. We cover stories like this every week. And you will not want to miss what comes next because the next part of this story completely rewrites what most people assume about Chicago's most famous food. Come join us. In 1943 in Chicago, a man named Ike Su, a former University of Texas football player turned liquor salesman teamed up with a friend named Rick Ricardo, an Italian-American artist and restaurant owner, to open a new business at the corner of Ohio and Wabash streets. Here is the detail that makes this strange. Su did not actually want to open a pizzeria. According to the story he told for the rest of his life, he originally wanted to open a Mexican restaurant, reasoning correctly that there was not a single decent Mexican restaurant anywhere in Chicago at the time. It was Ricardo, according to the popular version of events, who steered the concept toward pizza instead. And together, the two men built a restaurant, a pizzeria, out of a basement space that had previously housed a bar. What emerged from that kitchen in the closing months of 1943 was almost nothing like the pizza either Naples or New York's Little Italy had ever produced. A tall, buttery crust baked in a round steel pan built up the sides like the crust of a fruit pie, filled first with cheese, then meat or vegetables, and finally a thick layer of chunky tomato sauce poured on top instead of underneath and baked for nearly an hour instead of 90 seconds. This was not a faster, cheaper meal for laborers. This was a knife and fork dinner that took as long to cook as a roast. Ricardo, according to Rigus's research, had not set out to reinvent an Italian classic at all. He had simply inherited a basement kitchen that came with a leftover pizza oven and a stack of round cast iron pans left behind by the previous tenant, a tavern called the Pelican. And he built his new menu around the equipment already sitting in front of him. Cast iron pans hold and radiate heat far more slowly and evenly than a thin baking stone, which meant a crust baked inside one would never blister and char in 90 seconds the way a Neapolitan pizza does. It would need far longer in the oven, and a thin coating of dough would simply burn before the center ever finished cooking. So, the dough got thicker, layered with butter to keep it flaky rather than chewy, and pushed up the walls of the pan to hold everything inside. The order of ingredients flipped almost by necessity, too, because a thin layer of tomato sauce sitting directly on top of that much dough for nearly an hour would have reduced to a scorched bitter paste. So, the cheese went down first as an insulating layer, and the chunky, only lightly cooked tomato sauce went on last, protected from the worst of the heat. None of this was a conscious act of culinary rebellion against Naples. It was by most accounts a practical workaround built around the pans that happened to already be in the kitchen. The fact that it ended up looking and eating almost nothing like pizza was in a very real sense an accident of plumbing and cookware, not a grand artistic statement. Now, here is where the official Pizzeria Uno legend and the actual documented history start to pull apart. And it is worth sitting with because it tells you something important about how food origin stories get built in America. For decades, the story printed on menus credited Ike Su alone as the genius who invented deep dish pizza essentially by accident while trying and failing to build a Mexican restaurant. But a pizza historian named Peter Riggus spent more than a decade digging through primary sources, liquor license filings, partnership agreements, city records to figure out what actually happened at 29 East Ohio Street in the fall of 1943. What he found complicates the legend considerably. Liquor license paperwork signed by Ricardo in November of 1943 explicitly states that he had no partners. The original partnership agreement that would have made Su a co-owner was not signed until 1944. And even then, it was Su's wife, Florence, who signed it on his behalf, not Su himself. In other words, by the time Deep Dish Pizza was reportedly created, Su may not have had any legal ownership stake in the restaurant at all. Ricardo, who had discovered a leftover pizza oven and a set of round cast iron pans in the basement kitchen when he took over the space, appears to be the person who actually developed the deep dish recipe, training the restaurant's first cook personally, according to a Chicago newspaper article published within days of the restaurant's opening. A rival theory credits a later manager named Rudy Malnati, whose family would go on to found one of Chicago's other famous deep dish chains, but the timeline does not hold up. Melnati did not start managing the restaurant until 1951, 8 years after deep dish pizza was already being served. Whether Su, Ricardo, or someone else entirely deserves the credit remains genuinely disputed among historians. But one thing is not disputed. The version of the origin story that Pizzeria Uno told publicly for decades, a Texan liquor salesman single-handedly inventing an entirely new category of pizza was not just simplified. It was, according to the paperwork, largely built around a man who probably was not even a legal partner in the business at the time the recipe was created. Think about what that actually means for a moment. For roughly seven decades, millions of tourists sat down at Pizzeria Uno, read a menu that credited a single named individual with a singular flash of culinary genius, and believed it completely because there was no reason not to. It was a restaurant telling its own founding story, the same way countless restaurants do, and nobody thought to question it until one obsessive researcher started pulling liquor licensed microfilm out of the Cook County Archives decades later. That is worth sitting with because it says something about how easily an origin story can calcify into accepted fact simply by being repeated enough times on enough menus to enough hungry tourists who had no reason to doubt it. This is not a uniquely Chicago problem either. Food history is full of these tidy single inventor legends. Precisely because a clean story with one named hero is far easier to print on a placemat than an unglamorous truth involving a leftover pizza oven, a set of secondhand cast iron pans, and a chef whose own business partner eventually got most of the credit. Rudy Malnat's family, meanwhile, did not stay quiet about their own claim to the dish for long. His son, Lou Malnady, left Pizzeria Uno's orbit and opened his own restaurant under the family name in 1971. And Lou Malnadis has spent more than five decades since then, building an entirely separate deep dish empire. One that now operates dozens of locations and ships frozen pies across the country. Each one implicitly making its own quiet argument about whose family actually deserves credit for the crust inside it. Gordonos, founded by two Italian immigrant brothers in 1974, went a step further, introducing a stuffed version of deep dish with an entire second layer of dough sandwiched over the toppings, essentially escalating the original invention into something even further removed from anything Naples would recognize. By the 1980s, Chicago did not have one deep dish origin story anymore. It had several, each restaurant selling its own version of the legend along with its own version of the pizza. and tourists largely uninterested in untangling liquor license paperwork from 1943 simply picked whichever line was shortest. This is the part that should make you look at deep dish differently. What Su was undeniably brilliant at, whatever his actual role in the kitchen was marketing. At first, deep dish pizza did not sell. Chicago in 1943 had almost no reference point for what pizza was supposed to look like, let alone this strange tall casserole-like version of it. And customers simply did not know what to make of the thing being put in front of them. So Su, according to multiple accounts, gave away free samples of the deep dish pizza for months after the restaurant opened, essentially subsidizing an entire city's introduction to a food category he was in the process of inventing. Eventually, a newspaper reporter tried it, wrote about it enthusiastically, and the restaurant's fortunes turned. This was not about seasoning food or perfecting a recipe. This was about building an entirely new product category and then convincing an American city to want it. Deep dish pizza was not an accident that happened to be delicious. It was a deliberate act of product positioning built by men who understood that in a market with essentially no competition, whoever defined the category first would own it. And they named that category pizza, a word already carrying centuries of Neapolitan meaning and attached it to a dish that shared almost nothing with the original except the tomatoes and the cheese. Not the crust, not the cooking time, not the size, not the eating method. This was not a regional variation on pizza. It was closer to an entirely new dish wearing pizza's name, the way a company might launch a knockoff product under a trusted brand simply because the brand already had recognition built in. It worked spectacularly. Meanwhile, the broader trajectory of pizza in America was accelerating fast. Pizzeria Uno's popularity grew steadily through the late 1940s and into the 1950s. And Chicago's deep dish style began to spread through the city with imitators and successors developing their own versions and their own legends. Pizzeria duet opened one block from the original location in 1955 and other Chicago institutions. Lou Malnadis, Gordanos, Gino's East would go on to build their own competing deep dish empires in the decades that followed. Each claiming its own piece of the origin story, each fiercely defending its own version of what real Chicago pizza was supposed to taste like. This is where the story gets bigger than one restaurant. Across the rest of the country, pizza was industrializing along an entirely different track. And it is worth pausing on just how fast that happened. Frozen pizza entered American supermarkets in the 1950s, giving households a version of the dish they could keep in a freezer for months and cook themselves in 20 minutes. No restaurant required, national chains built an entirely new business model around pizza in the decades that followed, optimizing for speed and delivery rather than atmosphere or authenticity. first with din-in pizza parlors expanding into suburban strip malls through the 1950s and60s and then with a second wave built almost entirely around home delivery in the 1960s7s and 80s. This was pizza treated the way a manufacturer treats any product line. Standardized, franchised, and engineered for consistency across thousands of locations, so that a pizza ordered in one city tasted essentially identical to a pizza ordered a thousand miles away. Deep dish, by comparison, stayed a specialty item, a destination food, something tourists sought out specifically because it took an hour to bake and could not by its very nature be delivered quickly or eaten on the go. It became, in a strange twist, nobody could have designed on purpose, the anti- pizza. Everything mass market pizza was optimizing for speed, portability, low cost per slice, deep dish deliberately abandoned. And that refusal to industrialize the way the rest of the category did is a large part of why it still reads today as an event rather than a quick meal. This is the part that tends to catch people offguard because Chicago is far from finished with pizza's story of reinvention. In 2017, Neapolitan pizza making itself was granted UNESCO intangible cultural heritage status, an international recognition typically reserved for endangered traditions and cultural practices considered worth actively protecting. An organization founded in 1984, the Association Verace Pizza Napoleana enforces a strict almost legalistic definition of what counts as authentic Neapolitan pizza, specifying the exact type of flour, the exact fermentation time, the wood-fired oven temperature, even the diameter of the finished pie. Under these rules, deep dish pizza does not just fail to qualify as Neapolitan pizza. It fails to qualify as pizza in any traditional Italian sense at all. This is not exaggeration for dramatic effect either. It is a genuinely common opinion among Italian food writers, chefs, and ordinary Neapolitans who have publicly and repeatedly described Chicago deep dish as a casserole, a pie, or a tomato pot pie wearing pizza's name without earning it. The dish that once needed a queen's approval to become respectable in its own homeland is now in its most famous American descendant, considered by many of the people who invented pizza to not really be pizza at all. Here is a detail that would have been unimaginable to Rick Ricardo, Ike Su, or anyone eating pizza in the slums of Naples in the 1880s. In 2001, Pizza Hut became the first company in history to deliver a pizza off the surface of the Earth, sending a specially engineered 6-in pie up to cosmonauts aboard the International Space Station, developed in partnership with Russian food scientists specifically because a normal pizza would not survive the trip. Pepperoni was ruled out entirely for lacking the necessary shelf life in orbit. So, the crew received a cheese and salami version instead, vacuum-sealed and reheated on board. A marketing stunt certainly, but a genuine one, complete with its own small footnote in the history of human space flight. A food that once could not get a wealthy Neapolitan to admit he had eaten it, has since been sent into low Earth orbit as an advertising campaign. NASA has since funded its own research into three-dimensional food printers capable of producing a fresh layered pizza for astronauts on multi-year missions to Mars, squeezing dough, tomato powder, and a protein layer out of mechanical nozzles in an attempt to solve the exact same problem Neapolitan street vendors solved with nothing but flour and fire 250 years earlier. How to feed people something that tastes like home when almost nothing else around them does. And here is the detail that makes the whole story come full circle in the strangest possible way. Deep dish pizza today generates enormous revenue for Chicago's tourism economy with visitors specifically planning trips around eating at Lu Maladis, Gordanos, or the original Pizzeria Uno location, now a designated Chicago landmark. The broader American pizza industry, meanwhile, is valued at somewhere around 20 to nearly $40 billion annually, depending on which market analysis you trust. With Americans consuming an estimated 3 billion pizzas every single year, and roughly 1 in eight Americans, according to United States Department of Agriculture survey data, eating pizza on any given day. Deep dish is a relatively small slice of that enormous number, a specialty niche rather than the daily slice fast casual category that dominates the market. But its cultural weight is completely disproportionate to its market share because deep dish became something far bigger than a menu item. It became a mascot for an entire city's culinary identity. A food so distinctive that it launched and still fuels an actual ongoing rivalry with New York style pizza that plays out in restaurant reviews, late night comedy bits, and famously in a widely circulated remark from the chef and television host Anthony Bourdain, who once described deep dish only half joking as not pizza at all, but a kiche made in the wrong context. That kind of joke does not get made about food nobody cares about. It gets made about food that has become genuinely important to people's sense of place and identity. Food people are willing to argue about which is in its own way the highest compliment a regional dish can receive. It was there in the poorest slums of a chalera stricken Naples sold for pennies to people the wealthy would not look at. It was there when tomatoes, a fruit half of Europe still believed was poison, ended up on bread simply because hungry people had nothing left to lose. It was there in the streets of 1800's little Italy, carried across an ocean by immigrants who arrived to lynch mobs and newspaper headlines calling them racially suspect. It was there under curfew during a world war when the government of the very country falling in love with Italian food was locking up Italian fishermen as enemy aliens. It was there in the trenches and ration lines of that same war, tasted for the first time by American soldiers fighting their way toward Rome. It was there in a basement bar on Ohio Street in 1943, reinvented almost beyond recognition by a Texan who wanted tacos and a restaurant tour who found an old pizza oven in the kitchen he had just taken over. It was there in a decadesl long marketing legend that credited the wrong man or at least an incomplete version of the right one because the true story was messier and the mythology sold better. It was there in a family feud that split into three, then four competing Chicago dynasties. Each one certain its pan held the one true recipe. And it is there right now, tonight in your own city in two completely incompatible forms. On the one hand, a thin, blistered 92nd flatbread defended by international law and a strict Italian association with a name most people have never heard of. And on the other hand, a towering cheeses stuffed hour-long casserole that most actual Italians will tell you politely or not so politely does not deserve to share pizza's name at all. Both are called pizza. Both trace back, however loosely, to the same poor Neapolitan street vendors who first put tomatoes on bread out of pure necessity roughly 250 years ago. And both in their own completely different ways prove the same point. Pizza was never really about the crust or the sauce or the cheese or even the recipe. It was about who got to decide what the word meant. And it turns out that in America, all it ever took to redefine an entire cuisine was a good enough story and a name nobody thought to trademark. Not bad for a peasant flatbread that respectable Neapolitans once refused to be seen eating. If any part of this surprised you, the marketing legend, the lynching, the queen who may never have actually tasted the pizza named after her, let me know in the comments which detail got you. Because that is genuinely my favorite part of putting these videos together.
